entry.title: A Short Note of O(3) Frame

link.title: A Short Note of O(3) Frame

entry.content:
$$ \definecolor{input}{rgb}{0.42, 0.55, 0.74} \definecolor{params}{rgb}{0.51,0.70,0.40} \definecolor{output}{rgb}{0.843, 0.608, 0} \def\mba{\boldsymbol a} \def\mbb{\boldsymbol b} \def\mbc{\boldsymbol c} \def\mbd{\boldsymbol d} \def\mbe{\boldsymbol e} \def\mbf{\boldsymbol f} \def\mbg{\boldsymbol g} \def\mbh{\boldsymbol h} \def\mbi{\boldsymbol i} \def\mbj{\boldsymbol j} \def\mbk{\boldsymbol k} \def\mbl{\boldsymbol l} \def\mbm{\boldsymbol m} \def\mbn{\boldsymbol n} \def\mbo{\boldsymbol o} \def\mbp{\boldsymbol p} \def\mbq{\boldsymbol q} \def\mbr{\boldsymbol r} \def\mbs{\boldsymbol s} \def\mbt{\boldsymbol t} \def\mbu{\boldsymbol u} \def\mbv{\boldsymbol v} \def\mbw{\textcolor{params}{\boldsymbol w}} \def\mbx{\textcolor{input}{\boldsymbol x}} \def\mby{\boldsymbol y} \def\mbz{\boldsymbol z} \def\mbA{\boldsymbol A} \def\mbB{\boldsymbol B} \def\mbE{\boldsymbol E} \def\mbH{\boldsymbol{H}} \def\mbK{\boldsymbol{K}} \def\mbP{\boldsymbol{P}} \def\mbR{\boldsymbol{R}} \def\mbW{\textcolor{params}{\boldsymbol W}} \def\mbQ{\boldsymbol{Q}} \def\mbV{\boldsymbol{V}} \def\mbtheta{\textcolor{params}{\boldsymbol \theta}} \def\mbzero{\boldsymbol 0} \def\mbI{\boldsymbol I} \def\cF{\mathcal F} \def\cH{\mathcal H} \def\cL{\mathcal L} \def\cM{\mathcal M} \def\cN{\mathcal N} \def\cX{\mathcal X} \def\cY{\mathcal Y} \def\cU{\mathcal U} \def\bbR{\mathbb R} \def\y{\textcolor{output}{y}} $$

Data

We consider a centered point cloud $X \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times n}$ together with a connected graph $G$ whose nodes are the points and whose edges encode neighborhood or interaction structure. The graph $G$ come from a $r$-radius graph construction.

Our goal is to construct global or local orthonormal frames in $\mathbb{R}^3$ that depend on $(X,G)$ in an $O(3)$-equivariant way. Whenever a construction only yields a finite set of possible frames $\mathcal F(X) \subset O(3)$, we can enforce equivariance by averaging over this finite set \(\langle \Phi \rangle_{\mathcal F}(X) = \frac{1}{|\mathcal F(X)|}\sum_{g \in \mathcal F(X)} g \cdot \Phi(g^{-1}\cdot X),\) where $\Phi$ is a non-equivariant base model that consumes coordinates expressed in a chosen frame. The continuity and stability of $\mathcal F(X)$ with respect to small changes in $X$ are crucial for making this averaging practical.

Global Frame I: PCA-Based Frame Averaging

In the PCA-based approach, we construct a covariance matrix \(C = XX^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}.\) We then take its eigendecomposition \(C = Q \Lambda Q^\top,\) with $Q \in O(3)$ orthogonal and $\Lambda$ diagonal with non-negative eigenvalues. The columns of $Q$ are principal directions of variance in the point cloud. Because flipping the sign of any eigenvector leaves both $C$ and the orthogonality of $Q$ unchanged, there are $2^3 = 8$ distinct sign configurations that all represent valid orthonormal frames compatible with $C$. Thus, the frame set $\mathcal F(X)$ naturally includes all eight sign variants of $Q$, and we typically use frame averaging over these possibilities.

The main difficulty arises in degenerate or near-degenerate cases of the spectrum. If some eigenvalues are very small or zero, the point cloud is close to being planar or even linear. A zero eigenvalue means that all points lie in a plane (rank 2) or a line (rank 1), so the corresponding eigenvector is only defined up to any rotation in the null space. If eigenvalues are repeated, the eigenspace has dimension greater than one, and any orthonormal basis within that eigenspace is acceptable. These cases lead to infinitely many admissible frames $\mathcal F(X)$, and the choice of $Q$ becomes unstable: tiny perturbations of $X$ can cause large, discontinuous changes in the chosen eigenvectors.

This lack of uniqueness propagates to the frame averaging. The size and content of $\mathcal F(X)$ can change abruptly as the spectrum crosses a degeneracy point, making $\langle \Phi \rangle_{\mathcal F}(X)$ non-continuous as a function of $X$. For typical applications we focus on non-degenerate covariance, but in practice many datasets contain nearly planar or symmetric structures, so handling small or repeated eigenvalues is an important design consideration. Intuitively, zero or very small eigenvalues indicate that the point cloud has low variance along some directions, while equal eigenvalues indicate equal variance along some directions, which creates rotational ambiguity inside the corresponding subspace.

Global Frame II: Miminal Frame Averaging

Minimal frame averaging seeks the simplest possible global frame by choosing a small subset of points and orthonormalizing them. A typical construction is to select the first three non-collinear vectors among the columns of $X$, form the $3 \times 3$ matrix with these vectors as columns, and then apply QR decomposition to obtain an orthonormal matrix $Q \in O(3)$. This provides a candidate global frame that depends only on a few points.

This approach is conceptually simple and computationally cheap, but it is highly sensitive to the ordering and arrangement of the points. The frame depends on which three points are chosen, so it is permutation-dependent unless we impose a specific deterministic ordering rule (for example, sorting by some scalar feature). Once the order shifts under the rule, the frame changes abruptly. Moreover, if the selected vectors become collinear or nearly collinear, QR decomposition becomes ill-conditioned or fails to produce a stable basis.

These issues cause discontinuities in the induced mapping from $X$ to frames. As points move and cross collinearity thresholds, the frame can change sharply, which again leads to non-smooth behavior in any model that relies on this canonicalization. Frame averaging over the sign ambiguities of $Q$ can restore exact $O(3)$-equivariance, but it does not fix the fundamental instability coming from the discrete choice of which points define the frame.

Global Frame III: Learned Canonicalization

In learned canonicalization, the frame is not determined by learnable weights that depend on the data. A common idea is to produce three candidate vectors as weighted sums of the input points and then orthonormalize them. Concretely, one can define three sets of scalar weights ${\alpha_i^{(k)}(X)}_{i=1}^n$ for $k = 1,2,3$, and then form \(v_k(X) = \sum_{i=1}^n \alpha_i^{(k)}(X)\, x_i \in \mathbb{R}^3, \qquad k=1,2,3.\) Stacking these as columns gives a $3 \times 3$ matrix $V(X)$, and applying QR decomposition yields an orthonormal frame $Q(X)$. The weights $\alpha_i^{(k)}$ are produced by a neural network, typically designed to be permutation-invariant in $i$, so that the overall canonicalization is symmetric in the input points. Note that in this case, the number of $n$ is usually equal across samples.

This design allows the model to learn data-dependent directions that are optimal for the downstream task, but it inherits a similar degeneracy issue: if the three vectors $v_1, v_2, v_3$ become collinear or nearly collinear, the QR procedure is unstable and the resulting frame can change abruptly with small changes in $X$ or in the learned weights. In such cases, the effective size and structure of the admissible frame set $\mathcal F(X)$ can change, undermining the continuity and smoothness of the equivariant mapping. To mitigate this, one can add regularization terms that discourage degenerate configurations, for example penalizing small pairwise angles between $v_1, v_2, v_3$ or encouraging their norms and mutual orthogonality.

Local Frame I: Edge Frame

Local frames focus on neighborhoods, typically centered on graph edges or nodes. In the edge frame construction, we use the edge direction and cross products of associated vectors. Consider an edge $(i,j)$ in the graph with edge vector \(e_{ij} = x_j - x_i.\) We first normalize this to get a unit direction $u_1 = e_{ij}/|e_{ij}|$. To obtain a second direction, we select vectors $v_i$ and $v_j$ associated with the edge, for example positions $v_i = x_i$ and $v_j = x_j$, or another vectors incident to $i$ or $j$, and take a cross product: \(u_2 \propto v_i \times v_j.\) Finally, we can define a third direction as \(u_3 \propto u_1 \times u_2,\) and normalize all three vectors to get an orthonormal frame. In the language of spherical harmonics and irreducible representations, this construction can be seen as starting from $\ell=1$ vectors (the edge direction and another vector) and using their tensor product to generate new $\ell=1$ components, which are then orthonormalized.

The critical failure mode occurs when the chosen vectors are parallel or nearly parallel. If $v_i$ is parallel to $v_j$, their cross product vanishes, so we cannot construct a second independent direction. Even when they are only nearly parallel, $u_2$ has very small norm and is highly sensitive to noise, leading to unstable frames. As edges move or neighborhoods change, this can cause sudden flips or rotations of the local frame, which again compromises continuity.

Local Frame II: Edge-Pair Node Frame

An alternative local construction is based on pairs of edges around a node. For a given central node $i$, we consider all unordered pairs of incident edges $(i,j)$ and $(i,k)$. Each pair defines two edge vectors \(e_{ij} = X_j - X_i,\qquad e_{ik} = X_k - X_i.\) If these vectors are not collinear, they span a local plane, and we can use Gram–Schmidt to orthonormalize them into two unit directions $u_1, u_2$. A third direction $u_3$ is then obtained as $u_3 = u_1 \times u_2$, producing an orthonormal frame for that particular edge pair. The collection of all such frames over all pairs forms a local frame set $\mathcal F_i(X)$ at node $i$.

This method systematically explores the local geometry, but it has the same core degeneracy: when two edges are collinear, they fail to span a plane. In such configurations, the orthonormalization becomes ill-defined, and small changes in the positions of neighboring points can cause large changes in the selected frame. One common strategy is to assign weights to each edge pair, for example based on distances, and form weighted averages over the resulting frames or their induced features. We will discuss this in the next section.

Mitigating Discontinuity by Weighted Frame

A weighted frame averaging is frame averaging with input-dependent weights instead of a uniform average. Concretely, suppose we construct a finite set of frames \(\mathcal F(X) = \{g_1(X), \dots, g_K(X)\},\) where each $g_k(X)$ is a rotation. A weighted frame assigns nonnegative weights \(w_1(X), \dots, w_K(X) \quad\text{with}\quad \sum_{k=1}^K w_k(X) = 1,\) and then defines the symmetrized model as \(\left<\Phi\right>_{\mathcal F}(x) = \sum_{k=1}^K w_k(X)\, g_k(X)\,\big[\Phi\big(g_k(X)^{-1} X\big)\big].\) The important part is that both the frames $g_k(X)$ and the weights $w_k(X)$ are constructed from $X$ in a way that respects the group action and changes smoothly when $x$ changes. And the weights $w_k(X)$ vanish when $X$ is near degenerate. For example, to construct a smooth weight for radius graph construction, we can use a combination of smooth radial cutoff and smooth angular cutoff to detect graph construction changes and collinear vectors.

Proposal: Frame via Weighted Average

For each node $i$, we construct $v_1 = \sum_j a_{1,ij} e_{ij}$ and normalize it to get $u_1$. We then project all edges orthogonally to $u_1$, aggregate again $v_2 = \sum_j a_{2,ij} \left(e_{ij} - \left(e_{ij}\cdot u_1\right)u_1\right)$, normalize to get $u_2$, and set $u_3 = u_1 \times u_2$. With learned weights $a_{1,ij},a_{2,ij}$ and smoothed weights $w_i$ for degenerate cases of each node frame at $i$, this gives a node-wise orthonormal frame that is O(3)-equivariant, smooth in the coordinates, and only costs $O(\text{1})$ per node (no neighbor pairs, no eigen-decomposition).

Similarly, the same idea can be used for the global frame. We can construct $v_1 = \sum_{i}a_i X_i$ and normalize it to get $u_1$. We then project all nodes orthogonally to $u_1$, aggregate again $v_2 = \sum_j a_{i} \left(X_i - \left(X_i\cdot u_1\right)u_1\right)$, normalize to get $u_2$, and set $u_3 = u_1 \times u_2$. The frame is smooth and only costs $O(1)$.

entry.title: Accelerating Machine Learning Force Fields via Tensor Decomposition

link.title: Accelerating Machine Learning Force Fields via Tensor Decomposition

entry.content:
$$ \definecolor{input}{rgb}{0.42, 0.55, 0.74} \definecolor{params}{rgb}{0.51,0.70,0.40} \definecolor{output}{rgb}{0.843, 0.608, 0} \def\mba{\boldsymbol a} \def\mbb{\boldsymbol b} \def\mbc{\boldsymbol c} \def\mbd{\boldsymbol d} \def\mbe{\boldsymbol e} \def\mbf{\boldsymbol f} \def\mbg{\boldsymbol g} \def\mbh{\boldsymbol h} \def\mbi{\boldsymbol i} \def\mbj{\boldsymbol j} \def\mbk{\boldsymbol k} \def\mbl{\boldsymbol l} \def\mbm{\boldsymbol m} \def\mbn{\boldsymbol n} \def\mbo{\boldsymbol o} \def\mbp{\boldsymbol p} \def\mbq{\boldsymbol q} \def\mbr{\boldsymbol r} \def\mbs{\boldsymbol s} \def\mbt{\boldsymbol t} \def\mbu{\boldsymbol u} \def\mbv{\boldsymbol v} \def\mbw{\textcolor{params}{\boldsymbol w}} \def\mbx{\textcolor{input}{\boldsymbol x}} \def\mby{\boldsymbol y} \def\mbz{\boldsymbol z} \def\mbA{\boldsymbol A} \def\mbB{\boldsymbol B} \def\mbE{\boldsymbol E} \def\mbH{\boldsymbol{H}} \def\mbK{\boldsymbol{K}} \def\mbP{\boldsymbol{P}} \def\mbR{\boldsymbol{R}} \def\mbW{\textcolor{params}{\boldsymbol W}} \def\mbQ{\boldsymbol{Q}} \def\mbV{\boldsymbol{V}} \def\mbtheta{\textcolor{params}{\boldsymbol \theta}} \def\mbzero{\boldsymbol 0} \def\mbI{\boldsymbol I} \def\cF{\mathcal F} \def\cH{\mathcal H} \def\cL{\mathcal L} \def\cM{\mathcal M} \def\cN{\mathcal N} \def\cX{\mathcal X} \def\cY{\mathcal Y} \def\cU{\mathcal U} \def\bbR{\mathbb R} \def\y{\textcolor{output}{y}} $$

A machine-learning force field (MLFF) is a learned surrogate for quantum mechanics: you give it a 3D molecular structure, and it predicts the total energy and the force on each atom. This turns the expensive inner loop of atomistic simulation evaluating energies and forces thousands or millions of times into fast neural inference. When MLFFs are accurate and stable, they unlock longer and larger simulations for drug discovery (conformational dynamics, binding), materials design (electrolytes, catalysts), and process chemistry (reaction pathways), shifting work from supercomputers to commodity GPUs. Over the last few years, MLFFs have matured from “promising” to state-of-the-art on many benchmarks, with reviews chronicling how they frequently achieve sub-kcal/mol energy errors while rivaling or beating classical force fields in fidelity. To accelerate MLFFs, we introduce a faster way to build rotation-respecting models by replacing expensive tensor operations with a compact decomposition, cutting compute and memory and enabling larger models or more simulations at the same cost.

This post assumes you know basic graph neural network and point cloud modeling, but not deep knowledge in geometry deep learning.

Equivariance Challenge of MLFF

A central challenge in building reliable ML force fields is preserving equivariance. Unlike a vanilla graph neural network, a physically faithful model must respect symmetry by design: If you rotate a molecule in 3D space, its energy must stay the same (rotation invariance), and its force vectors must rotate exactly with the molecule (rotation equivariance). Just as in CNNs we want shift invariance/equivariance so that moving an object in an image doesn’t change recognition, here we want rotation equivariance so rotating a molecule doesn’t confuse the model. As CNNs encode translation equivariance, we encode rotation equivariance: rotating a molecule leaves scalar predictions unchanged and rotates vector outputs accordingly. If a model can guarantee that rotating the inputs predictably rotates the vector-valued outputs while leaving scalar outputs unchanged, it is formally SO(3)-equivariant (or SE(3)-equivariant if translations are also preserved). If rotating the inputs co-rotates vector outputs while leaving scalar outputs unchanged, the model is SO(3)-equivariant (SE(3)-equivariant if translations are also preserved). And an SO(3)-equivariant model should guarantee that rotating the inputs predictably rotates the vector-valued outputs while leaving scalar outputs unchanged. This isn’t just aesthetic correctness; it’s the difference between a network that memorizes poses and one that understands geometry.

Equivariance matters because it bakes physics into the architecture instead of hoping data augmentation will teach it. With only augmentations, the network sees many rotated copies and tries to learn the rule implicitly; with an equivariant design, the rule is hard-wired, so every layer preserves the symmetry exactly. In practice, this gives sharper generalization to new orientations and conformations, better data efficiency (you need fewer labeled geometries), and more stable molecular dynamics, because forces remain consistent as structures tumble and vibrate. Empirically, SE(3)/SO(3)-equivariant message passing has repeatedly shown improved accuracy and robustness across molecules, crystals, and surfaces.

The Canonical Recipe: Clebsch-Gordan Tensor Product

Having motivated why rotation equivariance matters, we now confront a limitation of conventional GNNs: they typically ingest Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ and process them with generic MLPs and message passing, which do not, by construction, respect SO(3). And the network must learn from data how predictions should transform under arbitrary rotations which is a hard, data-hungry problem. To make this symmetry explicit, instead of passing around $(x,y,z)$ vectors, we project geometric signals (e.g., relative positions) into a symmetry-aligned basis using spherical harmonics $Y_{\ell m}$, so rotations act as known linear transforms within each angular frequency. In this representation, enforcing or exploiting SO(3) equivariance becomes a matter of linear algebra rather than capacity, providing a clean bridge to the canonical receipt of equivariant operation: the Clebsch-Gordan (CG) tensor product.

Before we get into details of CG tensor product, we give a gental introduction to spherical harmonics. (Real) spherical harmonics $Y^\ell_m:S^2\to \mathbb{R}$ are functions defined on the surface of a sphere expanding spherical function $f:S^2\to \mathbb{R}$ as the angular Fourier expansion $f(x) = \sum_{\ell \ge 0}\sum_{m=-\ell}^\ell c_{\ell m} Y^\ell_m (x)$, i.e., any direcitonal signal on the sphere can be written as a weighted sum of these spherical harmonics on the unit sphere. The index $\ell$ (degree) sets how many bands/patches as the higher $\ell$, the finer the angular detail; while $m$ (order) rotates and slices that group of spherical harmonics around the axis. Low $\ell$ terms are very smooth (the average and a dipole), and higher $\ell$ terms add progressively finer structure, just like adding higher frequencies in a Fourier series. Practically, spherical harmonics give a compact, rotation-aware coordinate system for directions. If we have a function $f$ on the sphere, expanding it in harmonics is an angular Fourier series, as a few low-$\ell$ coefficients capture coarse trends, and more coefficients add detail.

For a concrete representation of spherical harmonics, let a unit vector $u = (x,y,z)$ and the corresponding spherical harmonics are polynomials of $x,y,z$ such that

\[Y^0_0(u) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi}}\] \[Y^1_{-1}(u) = \sqrt{\frac{3}{4\pi}}x, \quad Y^1_0(u) = \sqrt{\frac{3}{4\pi }}y, \quad Y^{1}_{-1}(u)=\sqrt{\frac{3}{4\pi}}z\] \[Y^2_{-2}(u) = \sqrt{\frac{15}{4\pi}}xz, \quad Y^2_{-1}(u) = \sqrt{\frac{15}{4\pi}}xy, \quad Y^2_0(u) = \sqrt{\frac{5}{4\pi}}(y^2 - \frac{x^2 + z^2}{2}), \quad Y^2_1(u) = \sqrt{\frac{15}{4\pi}}yz, \quad Y^2_2(u) = \sqrt{\frac{15}{16\pi}}(z^2 - x^2)\] \[\cdots\]

In principle, the \(Y^0 = \left(Y^0_0\right)\) is a scalar invariant to rotation, and \(Y^1 = \left(Y^1_{-1}, Y^1_{0},Y^1_1\right)\) is a vector equivariant to rotation. Each $Y^\ell$ will act as an element in CG tensor product and is called irreducible representation (irrep). To incorporate equivariance into models, most modern architectures represent features as irreps of SO(3) and combine them with CG tensor product that are symmetry-correct by construction. CG tensor product fuses irreps while keeping outputs in the right transformation class under rotation. Given spherical harmonics $Y^{\ell_1}$ and $Y^{\ell_2}$, CG tensor product tells us

\[Y^{\ell_1}\otimes_{CG}Y^{\ell_2} \to \{Y^\ell \}_{\vert\ell_1 - \ell_2\vert\le \ell\le \ell_1 + \ell_2}\]

that interacting between \(Y^{\ell_1}\) and \(Y^{\ell_2}\) can be decomposed into a series of spherical harmonics ranging from \(\vert\ell_1 -\ell_2\vert\) to \(\ell_1 + \ell_2\). For example, \(Y^1\otimes_{CG} Y^1\) can be decomposed into \(Y^0, Y^1, Y^2\), which are produced by inner product, cross product and traceless part of outer product of \(Y^1\) and \(Y^1\). These are all usual equivariant operations over Cartesian space and can be expressed within CG tensor product. Furthermore, each triplet \((\ell_1, \ell_2, \ell)\) is called a path. And given irreps $u,v$ and the tensor product result $w$, the concrete computation over each path $(\ell_1,\ell_2,\ell)$ is formulated as

\[w^\ell_m = \sum_{m_1 = -\ell_1}^{\ell_1} \sum_{m=-\ell_2}^{\ell_2} C_{\ell_1,m_1,\ell_2,m_2}^{\ell,m} u^{\ell_1}_{m_1}v^{\ell_2}_{m_2}\]

with $C_{\ell_1,m_1,\ell_2,m_2}^{\ell,m}$ the Clebsch-Gordan coefficient guaranteeing the SO(3) equivariance of the operation.

To model CG tensor product, it is common to set a maximum angular degree $L$ to features. Numerically, computing each path cost $\mathcal O(L^3)$ time complexity, and there exists $O(L^3)$ paths, so the number of “paths” that can couple input irreps grows quickly with the maximum angular degree $L$, and dense implementations scale as $\mathcal{O}(L^6)$. Overall, CG tensor product is elegant but quite computationally expensive.

Speeding Up Tensor Product via Tensor Decomposition

As we notice, the computation of CG tensor product is time-comsuming. By the universal property of the tensor product, any bilinear map $f$ factors uniquely through a linear map $M$ such that

\[f(u,v) = M(u\otimes v)\]

with $M$ a single contraction tensor transform the tensor product map of $u$ and $v$ to the output. In the CG settings, the tensor product on irreps is bilinear. Given input irreps $u,v$ and output irreps $w$, we collect all CG coefficients into a single 3-way CG tensor $M$ that maps “left irreps × right irreps” to “output irreps,”. Contracting $M$ with $u$ and $v$ yields the component of $w$:

\[w = M(u\otimes v),\]

which is exactly the universality of the tensor product applied to CG tensor product. Conceptually, we can collapse all computation paths into a single contraction $M(u\otimes v)$, which is simple to implement and highly GPU-friendly. In practice, the CG tensor $M$ is extremely sparse and contains repeated entries induced by the Clebsch–Gordan coefficients. For common numerical computation of tensor product, a direct way to do acceleration is tensor decompositionTensor decomposition is also called CP (CANDECOMP/PARAFAC) decomposition.. Inspired by this, we takes a clean, general idea from numerical linear algebra that approximating a 3-way tensor with a low-rank tensor decomposition to accelerate the CG tensor product. We then consider tensor decomposition factoring $M$ into a sum of rank-1 components such that

\[M_{kij} \approx \sum_{r=1}^R A_{kr}B_{ir}C_{jr}\]

where $A,B,C$ are factor matrices and $i,j,k$ are matrix indices. Computation then becomes three thin dense matrix multiplications and a Hadamard product instead of one huge sparse tensor contraction, such that

\[w \approx A(B^\top u\odot C^\top v)\]

Tensor decomposition has been a workhorse across signal processing and chemometrics for decades; its appeal here is that the speed/accuracy trade-off is controlled by the rank $R$. We then build Tensor Decomposition Networks (TDNs) by replacing each CG block with a rank-$R$ approximation and adding path-weight sharing so multiplicity weights are tied across all CG paths. We further provide theory: a uniform bound on the equivariance error induced by truncating to rank $R$, and a universality result showing that, as $R$ grows, the tensor-decomposition-based layer can approximate any equivariant bilinear map. Conceptually, TDN is a drop-in, “turn the crank” replacement for CG layers that trades a tiny, controlled equivariance error for big speed and memory wins.

Error–Speed Trade-offs and Large-Scale Molecular Study

Speed and throughput. At the operator level, we time a single tensor-product block with the same tensor shapes and irreps the network would feed it, and we compare the exact CG contraction against the tensor decomposition with the $R=7L^2$ policy. This isolates the cost of contraction itself, so no particular dataset loading, no other layers, and you see raw math and memory traffic over random generated samples. That’s where the escalating wall-clock factors come from $4.0\times, 4.8\times, 15.0\times, 26.7\times, 47.6\times, 83.6\times$ for $L=1\ldots6$. The growth is expected. A dense CG contraction scales roughly like $\mathcal{O}(L^6)$ when you account for the $\mathcal{O}(L^3)$ number of admissible paths and the $\mathcal{O}(L^3)$ work per path. The tensor decomposition alternative reduces the work to three skinny matrix multiplies plus a Hadamard product, which scales like $\mathcal{O}(R\cdot L^2)$. With $R\propto L^2$, the overall work becomes $\mathcal{O}(L^4)$, and the constant factors are friendlier: you replace many small, sparsely indexed reductions with a handful of cache-coherent GEMMs.

At the model level, we swap each CG block for its tensor decomposition counterpart and enable path-weight sharing. That changes two things at once. First, layers compute faster (the operator result above); second, the parameter count collapses from $\mathcal{O}(cL^3)$ to $\mathcal{O}(c)$ because multiplicity-space weights $c$ are tied across all CG paths. In our apples-to-apples runs comparing to Equiformer with standard CG tensor product, the end-to-end throughput moves from 311.7 → 770.8 samples/s at $L=1$, 71.9 → 312.4 at $L=2$, and 26.1 → 220.4 at $L=3$, while the parameters shrink from 12.1M/27.9M/54.7M to 4.5M across the same three settings. The constant 4.5M is a direct consequence of path-weight sharing: once multiplicity-space weights no longer multiply by the count of CG paths, increasing $L$ no longer balloons the parameter budget. In computational time, the gains come from three compounding effects: fewer FLOPs from $\mathcal{O}(L^6)\to\mathcal{O}(L^4)$, better arithmetic intensity because GEMMs reuse data in caches, and less indexing overhead since the tensor decomposition is contiguous matrix rather than many tiny, sparsely addressed reductions. The effect grows with $L$, which is exactly where vanilla equivariant models become least practical.

A massive real-world dataset. To move beyond toy problems, our study trains on PubChemQCR, a newly curated dataset derived from the PubChemQC project—a large quantum-chemistry database built from first-principles calculations. Each snapshot provides atomic numbers, 3D coordinates, the DFT total energy, and the per-atom forces; trajectories span a broad chemical space so the model sees both near-equilibrium and off-equilibrium configurations. On the Small split (≈1.5 M snapshots), TDN reports Energy MAE 4.46–5.01 meV and Force MAE ≈26.5–26.9 meV/Å on validation/test, outperforming a suite of competitive baselines. On the Full split (≈105 M snapshots), TDN achieves Energy MAE 1.50–1.65 meV and Force MAE ≈19.5–20.4 meV/Å. These numbers illustrate the central point: decomposed tensor products can preserve the accuracy practitioners expect while greatly improving computational efficiency, which is exactly what large-scale MLFF production needs.

What’s Next

Our low-rank tensor product is plug-and-play, but can be improved regarding engineering and hybridization. On the engineering side, we can move beyond generic PyTorch ops and build fused CUDA kernels that do the whole tensor decomposition step in one pass with shared memory, tensor-core GEMMs, and block-sparse layouts. That cuts kernel launches and data movement (the real time sink), lets us use mixed precision safely, and opens the door to auto-tuning rank $R$ per layer at runtime based on simple calibration batches. On the hybrid side, we can integrated tensor decomposition into existing fast equivariant tricks, e.g., pair it with cuEquivariance-style kernels, or with SO(2) convolution or Gaunt TP with FFT as long as they can be written in form of tensor product. Together we can push equivariant MLFFs to larger systems and longer trajectories without giving up the speed gains that make them practical.

$$ \definecolor{input}{rgb}{0.42, 0.55, 0.74} \definecolor{params}{rgb}{0.51,0.70,0.40} \definecolor{output}{rgb}{0.843, 0.608, 0} \def\mba{\boldsymbol a} \def\mbb{\boldsymbol b} \def\mbc{\boldsymbol c} \def\mbd{\boldsymbol d} \def\mbe{\boldsymbol e} \def\mbf{\boldsymbol f} \def\mbg{\boldsymbol g} \def\mbh{\boldsymbol h} \def\mbi{\boldsymbol i} \def\mbj{\boldsymbol j} \def\mbk{\boldsymbol k} \def\mbl{\boldsymbol l} \def\mbm{\boldsymbol m} \def\mbn{\boldsymbol n} \def\mbo{\boldsymbol o} \def\mbp{\boldsymbol p} \def\mbq{\boldsymbol q} \def\mbr{\boldsymbol r} \def\mbs{\boldsymbol s} \def\mbt{\boldsymbol t} \def\mbu{\boldsymbol u} \def\mbv{\boldsymbol v} \def\mbw{\textcolor{params}{\boldsymbol w}} \def\mbx{\textcolor{input}{\boldsymbol x}} \def\mby{\boldsymbol y} \def\mbz{\boldsymbol z} \def\mbA{\boldsymbol A} \def\mbB{\boldsymbol B} \def\mbE{\boldsymbol E} \def\mbH{\boldsymbol{H}} \def\mbK{\boldsymbol{K}} \def\mbP{\boldsymbol{P}} \def\mbR{\boldsymbol{R}} \def\mbW{\textcolor{params}{\boldsymbol W}} \def\mbQ{\boldsymbol{Q}} \def\mbV{\boldsymbol{V}} \def\mbtheta{\textcolor{params}{\boldsymbol \theta}} \def\mbzero{\boldsymbol 0} \def\mbI{\boldsymbol I} \def\cF{\mathcal F} \def\cH{\mathcal H} \def\cL{\mathcal L} \def\cM{\mathcal M} \def\cN{\mathcal N} \def\cX{\mathcal X} \def\cY{\mathcal Y} \def\cU{\mathcal U} \def\bbR{\mathbb R} \def\y{\textcolor{output}{y}} $$

Drug discovery is the process by which new candidate medications are discovered. Historically the drug discovery pipeline has relied on screening of large compound libraries followed by years of chemical optimization and clinical testing; success rates remain low and average costs can surpass billions of dollars. The recent advancement of machine learning contributes to substantially compressing the search space of candidate drugs and so that reduces the number of compounds that must be synthesized and the corresponding time and budget, though machine learning does not shorten the clinical phase time and regulatory requirements.

Pipeline of Drug Discovery

An industrial pipeline of drug discovery is commonly partitioned into four phases:

  • Early drug discovery begins by identifying a biological target (often a protein) whose altered activity is believed to influence a disease, and then searches chemical space for hits, compounds that modulate that target by high‑throughput robotic assays and computer‑based virtual screening with thousands to millions of molecules. Following this, medicinal chemists refine each hit’s structure to improve potency, selectivity, solubility, and preliminary safety in simple laboratory assays, yielding only a few hundred well‑characterized lead compounds.
  • Pre-clinical phase further refines and optimizes the candidate leads and conducts experiments in vitro (cell tests) or in vivo (animal tests). Compounds that fail on efficacy, bioavailability, or safety are discarded, so only several can survive and earn the data package needed to justify first‑in‑human trials.
  • Clinical phase unfolds in three numbered trials for the drugs from pre-clinical phase: Phase I, typically a small group of healthy volunteers, establishes a safe dose range and short‑term side‑effect profile; Phase II, first patients, provides the first evidence of efficacy; Phase III, a larger group of patients, confirms efficacy across varied populations and tracks less common adverse events, producing the complete risk–benefit dataset needed for marketing approval.
  • Regulatory review compiles all laboratory, animal, and human data into a New Drug Application (NDA) for small molecules or a Biologics License Application (BLA) for biologic therapies; agencies such as the FDA inspect raw data, and judge whether therapeutic benefit outweighs risk before granting or denying market authorization.

This top-down model is visualized in. Note that the overall attrition of this pipeline is steep because fewer than ten percent of lead candidates survive to approval, and every failure discovered late dramatically inflates cost.

Where Machine Learning Intervenes

Machine‑learning enters primarily in early drug discovery through target discovery, hit discovery, hit-to-lead and lead optimization, where data are abundant yet experimental cycles are costly and slow. Several key tasks of machine learning are included in each stage:

  • Target discovery identifies
  • Hit discovery
  • Hit-to-lead
  • Lead optimization

Scope of This Tutorial Series

Machine learning is not a replacement for biology, organic chemistry, or clinical insight, but it already reallocates experimental effort toward the most promising hypotheses. As foundation models scale and multi‑modal data sets expand—combining cryo‑EM structures, single‑cell omics, and longitudinal patient records—the fidelity of in silico predictions will rise. The long‑term goal is not merely faster discovery but a virtuous cycle in which every wet‑lab measurement feeds back to train models that, in turn, suggest better experiments.
